chapter_title: My Brother's Greatest Invention (Dreams and Discoveries)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.activity_title: Meet the Narrator and the Tinkerer

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read — pre-reading guess-the-invention paired activity (p.91).
Let us read — group discussion on a world without inventions (p.91).

time_bands.activity: Open with the paired guess-the-invention prompts from “Let us read” (p.91): students confer in pairs and share their guesses aloud. Encourage brief justifications for each guess.

Move into groups of four for the group discussion on what the world would look like without inventions and discoveries (p.91). Draw out a range of examples — food, medicine, communication — so students see how broad the idea of invention is.

Teacher reads the opening pages of the story aloud (p.91–96), students following in their textbooks. Pause after the burglar-alarm episode to let students react: ask who they think is more like Anand or more like Anita.

periods.teacher_notes: The pre-reading warm-up works best when pairs are given a genuine moment of silence to think before sharing; rushing to answers flattens the guessing game. A common early confusion is treating Anita purely as a disapproving bystander — the prose_summary makes clear she is a dry, observant narrator with her own voice, and drawing that out now pays dividends later.

periods.activity_title: The Time Machine and the Night Intruder

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss — cause-and-effect table for key story events (p.94).
Let us discuss — arrange story events in correct sequence (p.98).

homework.task_brief: Let us discuss — Did Anand keep his promise about the time machine? (p.94): write two to three sentences with reasons.

time_bands.activity: Continue the teacher-led read-aloud from where the story was left (p.96–101), covering the time-machine build, the parents' departure, the night Boppa appears, and the mystery ending. Students follow in their textbooks.

Work through the cause-and-effect table from “Let us discuss” (p.94) as a whole-class activity: teacher draws the table on the board, students call out causes and effects in turn, and the class evaluates each suggestion before it is recorded.

Students work individually to sequence the five story events from “Let us discuss” (p.98), then compare with a partner. Bring the class together for a brief oral debrief, asking students to justify each position in the sequence using story evidence.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read through the entire story, students are now ready to trace the narrative arc precisely; the cause-and-effect table rewards careful recall of details such as Anand rigging the burglar alarm to fire on a gentle push. The sequencing task often trips students on the final two events — Boppa locking them in and Anand misdirecting him — because the drama moves quickly; allow time for re-reading those paragraphs.

periods.activity_title: Reading the Extracts — Character and Atmosphere

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect — Extract 1: narrator's voice, tinkering, and Anand's personality (p.99).
Let us think and reflect — Extract 2: presence of mind, strange noises, and atmosphere (p.99–100).

time_bands.activity: Students re-read Extract 1 silently (p.99), focusing on what Anita reveals about herself and about Anand in the opening lines. Ask one student to read the extract aloud before the discussion begins.

Work through the Extract 1 questions from “Let us think and reflect” (p.99) as a guided class discussion: fill-in, multiple-choice meaning of ‘tinkering’, personality choice, and the comparative ECR question. For the extended response, take two or three oral answers and build a shared model on the board.

Students re-read Extract 2 (p.99–100) quietly, then work through its questions — fill-in on why Anita was angry, the presence-of-mind short answer, the cause-of-noises MCQ, and the atmosphere MCQ — in pairs before a whole-class check.

periods.teacher_notes: The Extract 1 ECR comparing Anita's and Anand's self-perceptions is the richest item here and benefits from a brief model before independent responses; the prose_summary notes Anita's dry, observational voice as distinct from Anand's confident self-belief, which students can draw on directly. The atmosphere MCQ in Extract 2 often leads students to choose only one word — emphasise that two descriptors can coexist in a single scene.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect — character-traits table with text evidence (p.100).
Let us think and reflect — short-answer story questions, items (i)–(iv) (p.101).

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect — short-answer questions (v) and (vi): why Sharma Uncle disbelieves Anand; write your own ending for Boppa (p.101).

time_bands.activity: Distribute the character-traits table from “Let us think and reflect” (p.100) orally: students pair up, choose traits from the box — creative, curious, careful, responsible, bothersome, confident — and match them to Anand and Anita with evidence from the text. Pairs share findings; teacher consolidates on the board.

Work through the first four short-answer questions from “Let us think and reflect” III (p.101) — what prompted the alarm, how Papa became its victim, how the family reacted to Anand’s ideas, and how Anand behaved on his inventing binges — as a guided discussion, with students writing brief answers in their notebooks as each is agreed upon.

periods.teacher_notes: The traits table rewards close reading: students sometimes confuse ‘curious’ and ‘creative’ and assign both to Anand without distinction; the prose_summary provides distinct evidence for each — curiosity is Anita’s questioning of the alarm, creativity is Anand’s sustained inventing. The two homework items are open-ended and need no prior class output; they stand alone.

periods.activity_title: Listening to a Martian and Sounding Out –ough

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen — choose true statements from the Anita-Toby conversation (p.105).
Let us listen — fill blanks with exact words from the conversation (p.105).
Let us speak — sort –ough words by pronunciation and share examples (p.105–106).

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the Anita-and-Toby transcript aloud at a measured pace (p.136), students listening with textbooks closed. After the first reading, teacher invites students to say what they understood about Toby before any questions are tackled.

Teacher reads the transcript a second time; students individually mark which of the five statements from “Let us listen” I (p.105) are true. Follow immediately with the fill-in-the-blanks activity (p.105) on a third reading, pausing briefly after each targeted phrase.

Transition to “Let us speak” (p.105–106): teacher models the pronunciation of ‘though’ and ‘enough’ from the story, then says each –ough word aloud. Pairs sort the words into pronunciation columns and share additional words they know; teacher confirms or corrects in a quick whole-class round.

periods.teacher_notes: The transcript is short enough to read three times in the time available; reading aloud rather than playing a recording keeps pace in the teacher’s control, which is important for the fill-in round. The –ough pronunciation sorting often surfaces regional accent variation — treat student suggestions as valid data for discussion rather than errors.

periods.activity_title: Describing a Vocation I Care About

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write — plan and draft a paragraph on a chosen vocation using given hints (p.106–107).

time_bands.activity: Open with a quick class brainstorm: teacher lists the vocations from the textbook on the board (electrician, mechanic, chef, nurse, graphic designer) and invites students to add two or three more from their own knowledge. Each student privately circles the vocation they will write about.

Teacher models a short paragraph on one vocation using the hints from “Let us write” (p.106–107) — showing how to move from ‘why I like it’ through tools and teamwork to how one would pursue it — writing the model on the board sentence by sentence and thinking aloud about transitions.

Students draft their own paragraph independently, using the hints as a guide. With a few minutes remaining, pairs exchange drafts and offer one compliment and one suggestion; writers make a quick revision before the end of the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: This writing task is self-contained: students choose their vocation, plan, draft, and do a peer-response round all within these minutes, so no carry-over is needed. Students occasionally write a list rather than a cohesive paragraph; the modelled example on the board should demonstrate how hints become connected sentences rather than bullet points.

periods.activity_title: Sound Words, Binomials, Phrasal Verbs, Idioms, and Tenses

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — match onomatopoeic words to their descriptions (p.101).
Let us learn — match words to form binomials; fill blanks with binomials (p.102).
Let us learn — fill blanks with correct phrasal verbs (p.102–103).
Let us learn — complete sentences with idioms from the given box (p.103).

homework.task_brief: Let us learn — fill blanks with simple past or past perfect form of verbs in brackets (p.104).

time_bands.activity: Begin with the onomatopoeia matching task from “Let us learn” (p.101): read each sound word from the story aloud — crash, humming, hissed, hammering/sawing/clattering — and discuss which description fits before students write matches. Link each word back to its moment in the story.

Move to binomials (p.102): teacher gives the example ‘peace and quiet’ from the text and explains the fixed-order rule, then students complete the matching task and the fill-in sentences in pairs before a whole-class check.

Work through the phrasal-verb fill-in paragraph (p.102–103) together: teacher reads the paragraph aloud with blanks signalled by a pause, students call out candidates, and the class discusses why each choice fits or does not.

Complete the idiom fill-in sentences (p.103) individually, then quickly share answers aloud. Teacher clarifies any idiom whose image students find puzzling — ‘get a shelling’, ‘leaving the coast clear’ — with a brief explanation of its origin.

periods.teacher_notes: Four vocabulary sub-tasks are anchored here; tense work (simple past / past perfect) moves to homework so neither set of items is rushed. Students frequently confuse ‘tripped off’ with ‘turned off’ in the phrasal-verb paragraph — pointing out that ‘tripped’ implies an accidental trigger (as in the burglar alarm) resolves the confusion through the story’s own context.

periods.activity_title: Indian Inventors: Discovery, Research, and Presentation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore — research Indian inventors not in the textbook and share with the class (p.107–108).

time_bands.activity: Open with a whole-chapter reflection: teacher revisits the chapter’s central ideas — the spirit of invention, the courage to fail and try again, the ambiguous ending — and connects them to the four Indian inventors named in “Let us explore” (p.107–108). Students briefly recall what struck them most across the story.

Students work in groups of three to brainstorm and note down the names and contributions of Indian inventors not listed in the textbook, drawing on prior general knowledge. Each group prepares a brief oral profile — name, field, and one key invention or discovery — to share with the class.

Groups share their profiles in a quick round-robin; teacher notes each name on the board to build a collective class list. Close by returning to Anand: ask the class what kind of inventor they think he might become, and what quality from the chapter’s inventor list he already shows.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws on the chapter’s themes — curiosity, imagination, determination — and the four textbook inventors (Sushruta, Dr. Janaki Ammal, Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, Dr. Narinder Singh Kapany) as springboards, so no prior research homework is required. The closing Anand question connects the fictional world back to real inventors and lets students synthesise the chapter’s ideas in a low-stakes oral form.

items.source_lo: Student reads and analyses a prose narrative to comprehend character, sequence events, and make inferences about theme and atmosphere using the prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Anand's inventions, burglar-alarm mishap, time-machine mystery, Boppa's disappearance, sibling dynamics.
items.item_stem:
Read the following passage and answer the question.

Anand had spent a fortnight in feverish activity, transforming his room into a network of wires, springs, levers, and bulbs. On the night their parents were away, a series of strange sounds — a tremendous crash, a scream, and muffled thumps — came from his room, after which the colony sweeper Boppa was nowhere to be found, leaving only his green scarf behind.

Which of the following best explains why Anand's time machine is described as his "greatest invention" in the story?

options.label: A
options.text: It was the most carefully designed of all his projects and worked exactly as planned.

options.label: B
options.text: It appeared to produce a result no one could explain — Boppa vanished without a trace.

options.label: C
options.text: It was the only invention that did not accidentally injure a family member.

options.label: D
options.text: It impressed Mr. Sharma, who publicly praised Anand for his scientific skill.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Suggests the student misread the story's tone — the prose emphasises Anand's impulsive style, not careful design.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Overlooks the burglar-alarm episode in which Papa was drenched, conflating 'greatest' with 'safest'.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Contradicts the text: Mr. Sharma dismissed Anand's claim and attributed the disappearance to imagination.

items.source_context: Anand's inventions, burglar-alarm mishap, time-machine mystery, Boppa's disappearance, sibling dynamics.
items.item_stem: In the story, Anita is the narrator and Anand is the inventor. Compare how each sibling responds to danger on the night Boppa breaks in. What does the way each character acts reveal about their personality? Support your answer with details from the story.

expected_elements: Anita notices danger first and wakes Anand — shows alertness.
Anand misdirects Boppa into his own room — shows quick thinking.
Contrast: Anita is cautious and observant; Anand is bold and resourceful.
Both responses reflect their established personalities from earlier in the story.

items.source_lo: Student listens attentively to a dialogue and demonstrates comprehension by identifying true statements and recalling exact words using the listening transcript as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Anita-and-Toby conversation: Martian physiology, sun-energy diet, one-eyed vision, pocket contents.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the conversation between Anita and Toby and then read the statements below. Write TRUE or FALSE for each statement.

1. Toby says he misses his people and home.
2. Toby tells Anita that Martians get their energy from eating fruit.
3. Anita is surprised to learn that Toby can see with his eye closed.
4. Toby says he can see that Anita is carrying a blue aeroplane in her pocket.
5. Anita says she cannot imagine life without ice creams and chocolates.

options.text: Toby says he misses his people and home.
Toby tells Anita that Martians get their energy from eating fruit.
Anita is surprised to learn that Toby can see with his eye closed.
Toby says he can see that Anita is carrying a blue aeroplane in her pocket.
Anita says she cannot imagine life without ice creams and chocolates.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — Toby says "I miss my people and home."
2. False — Toby says Martians get their energy from the Sun, not from food.
3. True — Anita gasps in disbelief when Toby says he can see with his eye closed.
4. True — Toby tells Anita he can see the blue aeroplane in her pocket.
5. True — Anita says "I can't think of life without them!"

items.source_lo: Student listens attentively to a dialogue and demonstrates comprehension by identifying true statements and recalling exact words using the listening transcript as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Anita-and-Toby conversation: Martian physiology, sun-energy diet, one-eyed vision, pocket contents.
items.item_stem:
After listening to Anita and Toby's conversation, answer the following question in one to two sentences.

Toby describes two extraordinary abilities his single eye gives him. What are these two abilities, and what does Anita's reaction — "Oh my goodness!" — tell you about how she feels at that moment?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Toby's single eye can see clearly even when closed, and it can see through mountains, clouds, woods, and metals — he tells Anita he can see the blue aeroplane in her pocket and describes the apple going round in her stomach. Anita's exclamation "Oh my goodness!" shows she is shocked and finds it almost impossible to believe.

items.source_context: –ough words from the story and speaking tasks: bough, dough, through, cough, thought, plough, pronunciation sorting.
items.item_stem:
Read each of the following –ough words aloud to your partner. Sort them into the correct pronunciation group by saying which sound the –ough makes in each word. The five sounds to sort into are: “oo” (as in blue), “off” (as in scoff), “o” (as in low), “ow” (as in now), and “aw” (as in saw).

Words to sort: through, cough, dough, plough, thought, bough.

expected_elements: Correctly sorts 'through' into the 'oo' sound group.
Correctly sorts 'cough' into the 'off' sound group.
Correctly sorts 'dough' into the 'o' sound group.
Correctly sorts 'plough' and 'bough' into the 'ow' sound group.
Correctly sorts 'thought' into the 'aw' sound group.
Speaks clearly and self-corrects after partner feedback.

items.source_lo: Student applies phonological awareness to sort and pronounce words with irregular spellings using oral pair-work as the vehicle.
items.source_context: –ough words from the story and speaking tasks: bough, dough, through, cough, thought, plough, pronunciation sorting.
items.item_stem: In the story, Anita mentions that the word 'enough' rhymes with 'puff', and 'though' rhymes with 'low'. Think about why the same letter combination –ough can be pronounced so many different ways in English. Share your opinion with a partner: do you think this makes English harder or more interesting to learn? Give at least one reason for your view, and use an example of an –ough word to support what you say.

expected_elements: States a clear opinion — harder or more interesting — with a reason.
Uses at least one –ough word correctly as an example.
Speaks in full sentences at an audible volume.
Listens to partner's response and acknowledges it briefly.

items.item_stem:
Choose ONE vocation from the list below. Write a paragraph of five to seven sentences about it. Your paragraph must include: why you find this vocation important, what kind of training it requires, and what tools or equipment are used in it.

Vocations: electrician, nurse, chef, mechanic, graphic designer.

expected_elements: Names the vocation clearly in the opening sentence.
States a specific reason why the vocation is important or appealing.
Mentions at least one aspect of training or qualification required.
Identifies one or more relevant tools or pieces of equipment.
Writes in connected sentences, not a list.

items.source_context: Vocation paragraph: why chosen, training, tools, teamwork, customer dealings, pride in work.
items.item_stem: Anand from the story loves tinkering with gadgets and dreams of being an inventor. Imagine you are Anand ten years later. You have now turned your passion for inventing into a real vocation. Write a paragraph in which you describe what your work involves, why you are proud of it, and how you handle a moment when a project goes wrong. Write in first person, as Anand.

expected_elements: Writes consistently in first person as an adult Anand.
Describes the nature of the inventing work with at least one specific detail.
Expresses a sense of pride in the vocation, linked to a personal value.
Addresses a setback or failure honestly and shows resilience.
Maintains a coherent paragraph structure with a clear opening and closing.

items.item_stem: Match each word or phrase from the story in Column A with its correct description or meaning in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
Column A|Column B
humming|a continuous low and steady sound
rigged up|put together quickly using available materials
get on one's nerves|to annoy or irritate someone
safe and sound|unharmed and out of danger
hissed|spoke in an angry whisper

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: humming – a continuous low and steady sound; rigged up – put together quickly using available materials; get on one's nerves – to annoy or irritate someone; safe and sound – unharmed and out of danger; hissed – spoke in an angry whisper.

items.item_stem:
Read the following passage about the night Boppa entered the house. Fill in each blank with the correct form of the verb given in brackets — simple past or past perfect.

By the time Anita (i) __________ (wake) Anand, she (ii) __________ (already / hear) the rattle at the door for several minutes. Anand (iii) __________ (jump) out of bed immediately. Earlier that evening, he (iv) __________ (set up) his time machine carefully before he (v) __________ (go) to sleep. When Boppa (vi) __________ (enter) Anand's room, he (vii) __________ (not / expect) to find the strange contraption that Anand (viii) __________ (build) there.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (i) woke (ii) had already heard (iii) jumped (iv) had set up (v) had gone (vi) entered (vii) had not expected (viii) had built.

items.item_stem: The chapter introduces four Indian inventors — Sushruta, Dr. Janaki Ammal, Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, and Dr. Narinder Singh Kapany. Research ONE Indian inventor who is NOT on this list. Prepare a short written profile (eight to ten sentences) that covers: the inventor's name and the time period they lived in, the field they worked in, their most important invention or discovery, and why their work matters today. Include at least one challenge they overcame.

expected_elements: Names a real Indian inventor not listed in the textbook.
States the field of work and time period accurately.
Describes the key invention or discovery clearly.
Explains at least one challenge the inventor faced.
States why the invention or discovery is still relevant today.

items.source_lo: Student researches and presents information about real-world inventors and innovations extending beyond the chapter's content using project-work as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Indian inventors: Sushruta, Dr. Janaki Ammal, Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, Dr. Narinder Singh Kapany; student-researched additions.
items.item_stem: Anand in the story never gives up — he moves from burglar alarms to a time machine to a telephone for outer space, each time undeterred by failure. Create an "Inventor's Comparison Chart" in which you place Anand (the fictional inventor) alongside ONE real Indian inventor of your choice. For each person, note: the invention they are known for, one quality that drove them, and one setback they faced. Then write three to four sentences explaining what both inventors have in common and what makes each of them unique.

expected_elements: Chart contains accurate information for both Anand and a named real inventor.
Identifies a shared quality — such as curiosity, persistence, or imagination.
Names a distinct setback for each person.
Written comparison distinguishes what is common from what is unique.
Uses information from research, not only from the chapter.
